WAIST-DEEP FLOODWATERS IN KAWIT, CAVITE Residents were forced to wade through chest-deep floodwaters along Toclong-San Sebastian Road and Tramo Street in Barangay Gahak, Kawit, Cavite after a nearby river overflowed amid continuous monsoon rains on August 8, 2026. Residents said flooding has become a recurring problem whenever heavy rains hit the area, raising concerns over the river’s capacity to carry water during prolonged rainfall. Some residents also pointed to structures along the river, which they believe may be obstructing the natural flow of water and contributing to the flooding. They are calling on authorities to conduct an inspection of the river and surrounding structures, identify possible obstructions, and take appropriate measures to help prevent or reduce flooding in the community. As heavy rains continue, residents are urged to remain alert, avoid wading through floodwaters whenever possible, and follow advisories from local authorities.  Photos by Rene H. LOOK:|BEHIND EVERY NUMBER: THE HUMAN HEARTBREAK OF NEPAL’S FLASH FLOOD. August 29, 2026 — One can scarcely imagine the terror: standing inside your own home, hearing the roar of water, mud, and rocks approaching — and having only seconds to wonder if your family will survive. That was the reality for communities along the Nepal–Tibet border on August 26, 2026, when a massive glacier and rock collapse triggered a catastrophic flash flood along the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi rivers. Homes, roads, bridges, power plants, and entire settlements were swept away — often with little or no warning.  IN THOSE FINAL MOMENTS Residents were forced to scramble to rooftops, balconies, or any higher ground available — clinging to hope as waters rose nearly 30 feet in half an hour. We may never fully know what went through their minds: Were they crying? Calling loved ones? Praying? Holding each other? What we do know is that behind every statistic is a human life, a family, and a story of heartbreak.  THE SCALE OF LOSS - 469 confirmed dead — and still rising - Hundreds more remain missing, including tourists and pilgrims from several nations - Entire communities buried under mud and debris - Rescue teams continue to reach isolated areas "Behind every number is a family waiting. Behind every missing person is someone desperately hoping. And behind every survivor is a story of courage."  May rescuers reach those still waiting. May the missing be found. And may every grieving family find strength in this time of unimaginable loss.  ,///Charlie. #PrayForNepal #NepalFlood #HimalayanDisaster #FlashFlood #DisasterAwareness #HopeAndPrayer #BosesNgPilipinas See less LOOK:|BEHIND EVERY NUMBER: THE HUMAN HEARTBREAK OF NEPAL’S FLASH FLOOD.

#1DNews | Davao, Philippines  FLOOD ALERT | Street Flooding Hits Carmelite Area in Bajada Following Hours of Rain LOOK: Residents of the Carmelite area in Bajada, Davao City, experienced street flooding early Wednesday, July 1, after several hours of continuous rainfall overnight. According to residents, flooding in the area is a recurring problem whenever heavy rains persist for more than two hours. As of this morning, floodwaters had reportedly risen from knee to waist level in some sections, affecting road access and threatening nearby homes, vehicles, and other properties. While residents noted that floodwaters typically recede within two to three hours after the rain stops, many continue to express concern over the recurring flooding and the damage it brings to their belongings and daily activities. Authorities are advising motorists and the public to exercise caution when passing through flood-prone areas. DAVAO: THE “FLOOD CAPITAL” — BUT PERHAPS NOT FOR THE REASON YOU THINK They say Davao is the “Flood Capital of the Philippines.” Well, if someone insists on giving us that crown, perhaps we should wear it proudly—but let’s first ask a simple question: What exactly is overflowing?  Yes, Davao experiences floods. We have rivers that swell after relentless rain, low-lying communities that sometimes bear the brunt of nature, sudden downpours that seem to arrive without an appointment, and roads that occasionally transform into temporary swimming pools. That is a real problem. It deserves real solutions—not political theater. But if we are going to compare cities, perhaps the scoreboard deserves more than a political slogan. During the severe southwest monsoon flooding in July 2025, for example, the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority reported hundreds of flooding incidents across Metro Manila within a single day. So before anyone points a finger at Davao, perhaps we should remember that flooding is not a problem exclusive to one city. Water does not check political affiliations before it rises. Rain does not ask who you voted for before it pours. And rivers certainly don't read campaign speeches.  But here's where I see Davao differently. Because there is another kind of flooding happening here—one that doesn't destroy homes, close roads, or leave mud behind. Davao floods with culture. Walk through this city and you encounter a living mosaic of Mindanao: Indigenous traditions, migrant communities, different languages, cuisines, beliefs, stories, and histories woven together into one constantly evolving urban tapestry. Ask someone where they came from, and you may discover an entire story behind the answer. Then, inevitably, there's food. Because in Davao, you can start a conversation about almost anything and somehow end up discussing durian.  “This variety is sweeter.” “No, that one has better texture.” “You haven't tried the best one yet.” Suddenly, what began as a casual conversation has transformed into an international conference on durian. No registration fee required.  But perhaps Davao's most remarkable flood is neither water nor culture. It is warmth. There is a quiet generosity in the character of many Dabawenyos that statistics cannot measure. You can arrive as a stranger and, before long, someone may already be telling you where to eat, what places to visit, which shortcut to take—and, most importantly, which road to avoid when traffic is terrible. That's not just hospitality. That's hospitality with a built-in traffic advisory.  And then there is Davao's natural beauty. The sea. Samal. Mount Apo. The forests. The farms. The rivers. The mountains. The wide spaces that remind you that progress and nature do not always have to be enemies. Davao is also changing. Businesses are arriving. Buildings are rising. Infrastructure is expanding. Communities are growing. People continue to come—not only because they are looking for jobs, but because they are looking for possibilities. Some arrive carrying résumés. Others arrive carrying business plans. Some arrive carrying nothing more than a dream. And somewhere along the way, many discover something unexpected: They don't merely live in Davao. They become part of it. That, perhaps, is the real story. A city should not be judged solely by the problems that rise within it. It should also be judged by what its people continue to build despite those problems. Davao is not perfect. We have traffic. We have growing pains. We have environmental concerns. We have infrastructure challenges. We have political disagreements. And, of course, we have social-media experts who can apparently repair the entire country using nothing but a smartphone and a Facebook account.  But beneath all the noise is something far more difficult to construct: Character. You can build a highway. You can build skyscrapers. You can build malls, bridges, offices, and massive developments. You can even build a spectacular roundabout that everyone will complain about for months.  But you cannot manufacture belonging. You cannot pour it into concrete. You cannot buy it from a catalog. It has to grow. And Davao has grown through people. People from different places came here. They planted roots. They built families. They opened businesses. They raised children. They created communities. And little by little, their individual stories became part of the larger story of the city. For the past 15 years, I have had the privilege of traveling around Davao for team-building activities, retreats, seminars, workshops, and speaking engagements. And in those years, I have seen something that no flood statistics can capture. I have seen people flood others with smiles, generosity, and warmth. The storm will begin weakening prior to landfall along our coast this evening, but it will still be a SIGNIFICANT hurricane upon impact. The worst conditions are expected from late afternoon through late evening as the center makes landfall, likely between Mobile Bay and Choctawhatchee Bay.  Storm Surge: Potential for 6-9 feet for the western Florida Panhandle, 4-6 ft for the Alabama coastline, and 3-5 ft for Mobile Bay. Surge will be highest near and east of the track, while areas west of the track may experience low water levels around landfall.  Winds: Upon approach, widespread tropical storm force winds and wind damage will occur well away from the center, with damaging hurricane-force winds near the center close to the coast. Expect winds to cause structural damage and knock down trees/powerlines, leading numerous power outages.  Flooding: Heavy rain near the core of the storm and in bands well east of the center could cause significant flash flooding, especially on saturated ground and in urban areas. Storm total rainfall amounts, generally around 4-8 inches for areas east of the Alabama River; highest by the coast. Localized totals up to 12 inches are possible, particularly near/just west of the track.  Tornadoes: An increased threat of several tornadoes exists late afternoon into tonight for areas east of I-65 within the outer bands. Then May 18 to May 19 halos tuloy tuloy na ang moderate to heavy rain with thunderstorms and flood advisories especially sa low-lying areas. As in HOURS yung ulan, hindi yung typical na “saglit lang naman umulan.” Pero pagdating online, parang nawalan lahat ng common sense  Suddenly: “Davao can never.” “Singapore nga hindi binabaha.” “51 billion flood control nasan na?” “DDS delusion.” “Supercity pero bahain.” Like damn, everybody became engineers, meteorologists, and urban planners overnight  Nobody is saying “okay lang ang baha.” Of course frustrating siya. Residents were affected. Motorists and commuters got stranded. Valid lahat ng reklamo about needing better drainage, better urban planning, and better maintenance. Pero ang weird kasi some people are acting like: 1. walang nonstop heavy rain for almost 2 to 3 days 2. walang low-lying flood-prone areas 3. walang factor ang geography ng Davao at parang unique sa Davao ang flooding during extreme weather People also keep screaming about the “₱51 billion flood control” without even reading the actual reports   Even clarified na hindi yan purely flood control. Kasama diyan roads, bridges, bypass roads, coastal roads, drainage works, river defense projects, and other infrastructure allocations from 2020–2022. Hindi yan parang: insert ₱51B charaaaan flood immunity unlocked! And about geography, people forget na Davao catches runoff from the Mt. Apo system and even southeastern Bukidnon. text: "OO, RESIDENTE AKO NG DAVAO CITY"  Kinuwestiyon ni dating Philippine National Police (PNP) Chief Nicolas Torre III ang patuloy na pagbaha sa Davao City matapos muling bahain ang kanyang bahay sa NHA Bangkal, Barangay Talomo kasunod ng malakas na ulan noong Hulyo 24. Sa kanyang social media post, sinabi ni Torre na nakapangalan sa kanya at sa kanyang asawa ang naturang bahay at bilang residente ng Davao City ay may karapatan siyang magtanong kung bakit paulit-ulit pa ring nangyayari ang pagbaha. Ayon kay Torre, matagal nang alam na ang mga sanhi ng pagbaha tulad ng mountain runoff at malalakas na pag-ulan, kaya dapat aniya ay may epektibong solusyon na, lalo na't bilyon-bilyong piso na ang nagastos para sa mga flood control projects. Binigyang-diin niya na ang tunay na sukatan ng flood control ay hindi ang dami ng proyektong naipatupad kundi ang dami ng pamilyang hindi na naaabot ng baha.
